title: ACT Pronoun Case: I or Me, Who or Whom
summary: Subject, object and possessive pronouns — pairs like “my sister and I”, “between you and me”, pronouns after than/as, who vs whom and whoever vs whomever — with worked examples and an ACT-style quiz.

blocks.text: “My friend and me went…”, “between you and I…”, “the man who I met…” — all three sound normal in everyday speech, and all three are wrong in Standard English. Pronoun case questions test whether you choose the **subject form**, the **object form** or the **possessive form** of a pronoun. The ACT likes them because your ear cannot be trusted. This lesson gives you a quick test for every case the exam uses.
What this question type tests

Pronoun case is part of **Conventions of Standard English**, which is **38–43%** of the 40 scored English questions (shared with punctuation, sentence structure and the other usage topics). A pronoun — often with another noun, such as “my sister and **I**” — is underlined, and the choices offer different forms: **I / me / myself / mine**, **he / him / his**, **who / whom / whose**, **whoever / whomever**.

When the vertical scan shows the choices changing only the pronoun’s form, ask one question: **what job does the pronoun do in its own clause?** Does it do the action (subject), receive the action or follow a preposition (object), or own something (possessive)?
The three cases

headers: Object form (receives the action / after a preposition)

items: **Subject form** before a verb: ✓ **She** won. ✓ **They** were late.
**Object form** after a verb: ✓ The coach chose **him**. After a preposition (to, for, with, between, among, about, except, like, from, behind): ✓ for **her**, with **them**, between **us**.

**Possessive** forms never take an apostrophe: ✓ **its** roof, **theirs**, **yours**, **whose** idea. ✗ it’s roof, their’s, your’s, who’s idea. (it’s = it is / it has; who’s = who is / who has; they’re = they are.)

blocks.text: Rule 1: Compound pronouns — cover the other person

Most case errors happen when a pronoun is joined to a noun with **and** or **or**. Cover the noun and the “and”, then read the pronoun alone. The form that works alone is the form that works in the pair.

rows: The letter was for my parents and **we**.
The letter was for my parents and **us**.
**Him** and his cousin opened a shop.
**He** and his cousin opened a shop.
Between you and **I**, the plan won’t work.
Between you and **me**, the plan won’t work.

blocks.text: “Between you and I” sounds polite and formal, which is exactly why it is a trap. **Between** is a preposition, so **both** pronouns after it must be object forms: between you and **me**, between **him** and **her**, between **us** and **them**.

**Pronoun + noun (we students / us students):** drop the noun and test. ✓ **We** students organised the fair (We organised…). ✓ The principal praised **us** students (praised us). ✗ **Us** students organised the fair.

**Appositives:** when a pronoun renames a noun, it takes the case of that noun. ✓ Two members, Laila and **I**, gave the speech (subject). ✓ The judges chose two members, Laila and **me** (object of “chose”).

blocks.title: غطّي الاسم التاني
blocks.text: لو قدامك my sister and I/me، غطّي my sister and واقرأ الضمير لوحده. لو الجملة بقت "Me cooked dinner" يبقى غلط، والصح I. وبعد حروف الجر زي between و for و with دايمًا me / him / her / us / them. يعني between you and **me** مش between you and I.
Rule 2: Reflexive pronouns (myself, himself…)

A reflexive pronoun is correct only in two situations: (1) the subject does the action **to or for itself**, (2) for **emphasis** right after the noun. It can never replace I or me just because it sounds more polite.

rows: Please send the forms to Mona or **myself**.
Please send the forms to Mona or **me**.

blocks.text: Rule 3: After than and as — finish the sentence
After **than** or **as** in a comparison, a verb is usually missing. Add it back, and the correct pronoun becomes clear.

items: ✓ My brother is taller than **I** (am). ✗ My brother is taller than **me** am.
✓ Nobody in the class worked as hard as **she** (did).
✓ The news surprised my father more than (it surprised) **me**.
The meaning can change: “Ahmed likes Omar more than **I**” = more than I like Omar. “Ahmed likes Omar more than **me**” = more than he likes me.

blocks.text: On the ACT the safest answer is often the version that **writes the verb in**: “than **I am**”, “as **she did**”. If a choice gives “than me did” or “than myself”, it is wrong.
Rule 4: Possessive before an -ing word

When a pronoun comes right before a gerund (an -ing word used as a noun), Standard English prefers the **possessive** form, because the gerund is a thing. ✓ We were surprised by **his** winning the race. ✓ The coach did not like **our** arriving late. ✗ The coach did not like **us** arriving late. (The coach does not dislike *us*; he dislikes the arriving late.)
Rule 5: Who or whom? The he/him test
**Who** is a subject form (like **he**); **whom** is an object form (like **him**). Both end in -m: **whom = him**. To decide:

items: Take the clause that starts with who/whom and stop at its end.
Rearrange it into a short sentence and put **he** or **him** in place of who/whom.
If **he** fits → **who**. If **him** fits → **whom**.

rows: The engineer ___ designed the bridge retired.
The engineer ___ the city hired retired.
To ___ did you give the key?
She is the author ___ I wrote to.

items: **Right after a preposition, always whom:** ✓ the friend **with whom** I travelled; ✓ the people **for whom** the hospital was built; ✗ to who, for who, with who.
**Ignore “I think / she believes / they say” inside the clause:** “The girl ___ I think won the prize” → cross out “I think” → **she** won the prize → **who**. This is the most common who/whom trap.
**Whose** shows possession and is followed by a noun: the farmer **whose** land flooded. **Who’s** = who is / who has.
**Which** is for things and animals, never for people: ✗ the doctor **which** helped us ✓ the doctor **who** helped us.

blocks.text: Rule 6: Whoever or whomever?

Whoever/whomever begins a clause, and its case depends **only on its job inside that clause** — not on the word before it. A preposition in front of the clause does **not** make it “whomever” automatically.

rows: Give the prize to ___ finishes first.
**he** finishes first (the whole clause is the object of “to”)
___ wins the vote will lead the club.
The coach will pick ___ she trusts most.

blocks.title: Who ولا Whom؟
blocks.text: حوّل الجملة الصغيرة لجملة عادية وجرّب he و him. لو he مناسبة استخدم who، ولو him مناسبة استخدم whom (الاتنين آخرهم m). وبعد حرف جر على طول (to / with / for) دايمًا whom. لكن whoever و whomever بتتحدد من جملتها هي بس: to whoever finishes first لأن he finishes.
Worked examples
Each example is part of an ACT-style essay. The underlined portion is shown in **bold**.
**Worked example 1.** “When the concert was cancelled, the manager gave the last two refund vouchers to my cousin and **I**.”
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) me
C) myself
D) mine

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** Cover “my cousin and”: the manager gave the vouchers “to **me**”. After the preposition “to”, the object form is needed.
**A** is the subject form — the “sounds polite” trap.
**C** is reflexive, but the subject (the manager) is not the person receiving the vouchers.
**D** is a possessive (“mine” = my thing), which makes no sense here.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2.** “The scientist **who** the committee selected for the award had studied coral reefs in the Red Sea for twenty years.”
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) whom
C) whose
D) which

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** Make the clause a sentence: “the committee selected **him**” → him = whom. The scientist is the object of “selected”.
**A** is the subject form; it would only fit if the scientist did the selecting.
**C** shows possession and needs a noun after it (whose research…).
**D** is used for things, not people.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3.** “My grandmother is seventy-four, but on our morning walks along the Corniche she still moves faster **than me**.”
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) than I do
C) then I do
D) than myself

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** Finish the comparison: she moves faster than **I** (move). Writing the verb in — “than I do” — makes the subject form necessary and clear.
**A** uses the object form where the sentence needs a subject for the missing verb.
**C** uses “then”, a time word, instead of “than”, the comparison word.
**D** uses a reflexive pronoun without a matching subject.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4.** “The school will publish the winning story in its magazine, and the prize will go to **whomever** writes the most original ending.”
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) whoever
C) whom
D) themselves

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** Look only inside the clause: “___ writes the most original ending” → **he** writes → whoever. The whole clause is the object of “to”, but whoever is the subject of “writes”.
**A** is the classic trap: students see the preposition “to” and choose the object form.
**C** is also an object form, and “to whom writes” is not a sentence.
**D** is a reflexive pronoun with nothing to refer back to.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **Sounds-polite trap:** “between you and I”, “for Mona and I”, “Karim and myself” — all wrong.
**Pronoun at the start of a pair:** “Him and his brother went…” → He and his brother went…
**Than me / as him** where a verb is understood: write the verb in and the subject form appears (than I am).
**Who after a preposition:** to who, with who → to whom, with whom.
**I think / she said inside the clause:** cross it out before the he/him test (the girl who I think won…).
**Whomever after a preposition:** the case comes from the clause (to whoever finishes), not from “to”.
**Apostrophe possessives:** it’s, their’s, who’s, your’s are never possessive forms.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Pair of pronouns or names? Cover the other person and read the pronoun alone.
After a preposition (between, for, to, with, among, except)? Object form: me, him, her, us, them, whom.
who/whom/whoever/whomever? Rewrite the clause with he/him. he → who; him → whom.
than / as? Add the missing verb in your head.
Reflexive (myself) only if the same person is already the subject, or for emphasis.

blocks.text: Practice
Two ACT-style essays with 5 questions each, all on pronoun case. The numbers in brackets match the question numbers.

blocks.title: Pronoun Case quiz
blocks.intro: Two ACT-style essays with 5 questions each. For every underlined pronoun, decide its job in its own clause: subject, object or possessive.

questions.p:
The Robot in the Kitchen

Last spring, my older brother Omar decided to build a robot for the regional science fair. Our father is an engineer, and he offered to help, but Omar wanted the project to belong only to __him and I__ [1]. I was his one and only assistant, and I took the job very seriously.

For three weeks the kitchen table disappeared under wires, batteries and tiny motors. Omar was far more patient __than me__ [2]. When a motor burned out, he simply started again, while I wanted to give up. Our neighbor, __who__ [3] had once worked in a car factory, lent us a small gearbox and showed us how to fit it inside the robot's body.

On the day of the fair, the judges asked to speak with the two builders, Omar and __I__ [4]. Between you and __me__ [5], I was terrified, but Omar did most of the talking. We did not win first prize. We came home with a certificate, a lot of advice and a robot that can still carry a cup of tea across the kitchen without spilling a drop.
questions.q: [1] Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: Both pronouns follow the preposition “to”, so both must be object forms: “to him and me”. Test by covering: “belong to I” is wrong. A and B use the subject form “I” (B also uses “he”); D uses a reflexive pronoun with no matching subject.

questions.p:
The Teacher Who Answered Every Letter

In 1998, a schoolteacher in Aswan named Hoda Mansour began writing letters to classes in other countries. The pupils to __who__ [6] she wrote were children of her own students' age in Canada, Japan and Brazil. She answered every letter she received by hand, even though some of them took two months to arrive. Within a year, the replies filled a whole drawer of her desk.

Over the years, her classes joined in. Each autumn, she told her pupils that they could write to __whoever__ [7] they wanted, as long as the letters were polite and true. Some chose astronauts and footballers. Others chose authors __who's__ [8] books they had read in class.

Hundreds of the replies are still kept in a cardboard box in the school library. For __us__ [9] students who read them today, the box is a kind of time machine. The pupil __whom__ [10] the librarian believes received the most replies was a shy boy named Karim. He wrote to twelve scientists, and every one of them wrote back.
questions.q: [6] Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: Right after a preposition (“to”) the object form is needed: “to whom”. Test: she wrote to **him**. A is the subject form; C shows possession and needs a noun; D is not used for people.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Subject forms (I, he, she, we, they, who, whoever) do the action; object forms (me, him, her, us, them, whom, whomever) receive it or follow a preposition.
In a pair, cover the other person: “Karim and I went”, “for Karim and me”, “between you and me”.
After than/as, add the missing verb: taller than I (am).
who/whom: he → who, him → whom; ignore “I think” inside the clause. whoever/whomever: test inside its own clause only.
Possessives have no apostrophe (its, whose, theirs); reflexives (myself) only when the subject acts on itself or for emphasis.
